speech from mixed audio. By modeling a speaker's semantic concepts, such as
their age, gender, and accents, we can better model the underlying speech
mixing process and improve separation performance. Our proposed network
incorporates a novel memory-based attention mechanism that allows for the
efficient combination of semantic concepts in the separation process. We
evaluate our method on the Wall Street Journal speech dataset and demonstrate
superior results compared to existing methods.

Quantum parameter estimation tasks can be optimized using a unique property called block coherence. We've developed a method based on random block decomposition, which allows us to determine the optimal block size for any given state and measurement type. Our technique also enables the creation of customized states with predetermined block coherence values. Furthermore, we've successfully applied this approach to optimize quantum parameter estimation in various scenarios, including inhomogeneous magnetic fields and frequency shifts.

Our research has provided a comprehensive analysis of the source H 1743-322 across 1.3-50 T Hz during its 2017 state transition, a period marked by a sharp drop in its hard X-ray flux. The data collected by AstroSat's spectrometry and soft X-ray monitors have been complemented by high-energy data from Insight-HXMT and Fermi-LAT. The resulting multi-wavelength spectrum reveals a complex pattern of a broad thermal disk component, a broadened thermal disk reflection feature, and non-thermal emission processes. The analysis of the data suggests that the source's emission is predominantly non-thermal in nature, a characteristic consistent with previous observations of its outbursts. The analysis of the data also reveals a correlation between the source's quasi-periodic oscillations and its non-thermal emission, indicating that the latter is influenced by the former. The study's findings are consistent with the notion that the majority of its emission is non-thermal in nature, a characteristic observed across different outbursts of the source, including the one in 2017.

A highly adaptable and efficient question-answering model is presented, capable of providing accurate responses to a wide range of questions on various subjects, including topics such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The model leverages pre-trained BERT embeddings combined with frequency-based word importance and a hierarchical attention mechanism to process queries. The model's parameters are efficiently shared across multiple topics, resulting in significant reductions in parameter count. The proposed method yields pre-trained models that generalize well across multiple topics and can be easily adapted to new topics with minimal training data, showcasing good performance even when there are few training examples. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through evaluation on the COVID-19 Q&A dataset, where it surpasses the performance of a co-trained model and a multi-task model.

The origin of the Warm Hot Intergalactic Medium's (WHIM) heating is still unclear.
We used the IllustrisTNG-100 simulation to explore how galactic outflows and
accretion shocks contribute to WHIM heating. We found that outflows primarily heat
the hottest WHIM phases, whereas cosmic shocks are more effective at heating the
coldest phases. The most massive filaments, with temperatures above 10^7 K,
originate from outflows. The cosmic shocks are found in larger scale structures.
Outflow-heated gas tends to be more diffuse and follows smaller-scale filaments,
whereas shock-heated gas is more compact and follows larger-scale filaments.
The outflows' impact is most evident within 1-10 Mpc of their host galaxies.
The limited resolution in current WHIM studies means they can't distinguish between
outflow and shock heating.

We introduce the concept of a "leftmost" separator that splits a graph's vertices A and B by finding the smallest set of edges i from 1 to k that separates A and B, where separation occurs earliest for k. We explore the computational complexity of determining whether a graph can be divided into two sets of non-negative weights, where each subset of vertices can be separated by a "leftmost" separator of at most k edges, and can be either be done efficiently or has no known efficient solution.

We've developed a new method using deep learning to identify Tidal Disruption Events (TDEs) in light curves from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Zwicky Survey (iPTF), which will help us precisely classify TDEs and detect other transient phenomena. Our approach involves a two-stage process: first, separating TDEs from other variables like active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and stellar variable stars, and then distinguishing between TDEs and other transient events like Type Ia supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. We've tested our method using a combination of real and simulated data, demonstrating its effectiveness in distinguishing TDEs from other variables and accurately categorizing different types of transients. Our results show that our method can accurately detect TDEs in real data, and it will be an essential tool for analyzing future data sets as they become available.

This study examines the challenges of providing Quality of Service (QoS) support in complex reconfigurable wireless networks (RWNs) that involve numerous interconnected nodes with adjustable features such as transmission power, frequency usage, and resource allocation. A key challenge in these networks lies in their ability to dynamically change network resources, which can lead to network congestion and resource depletion. To address these issues, we propose a novel architecture called the RWN QoS Game Engine (RWN-QGE) that enables nodes to make informed decisions regarding QoS allocation and resource management. A mathematical model is developed to describe the behavior of each node, and we validate its accuracy through a theoretical analysis. To test the effectiveness of the RWN-QGE, we conduct extensive simulations, which demonstrate its ability to provide high-quality services to network users under diverse conditions. The results of our study can contribute to the development of advanced mobile networks, such as 6th generation (6G) networks, that provide AI-driven QoS support for a wide range of applications.

In machine translation assisted by humans, certain techniques can improve
alignment between unaltered source and edited target words. However, these methods
fall short when dealing with words that are added or modified in the editing process.
To address this limitation, we propose an approach that leverages editing data
to align both modified and original target words with their source counterparts. 
Our evaluation on multiple tasks indicates that this method effectively expands the
scope of word alignment without compromising performance in existing tasks.

This study focuses on rotating black holes within the context of $f(\mathcal{R})$ gravity, specifically the modified gravity theory $f(\mathcal{R}) = \mathcal{R} + m^2 \log \log(\alpha + \frac{\mathcal{R}}{M^2})$, where $\mathcal{R}$ represents the Ricci scalar, $m$ and $M$ are parameters with specific values. The research explores the properties of these black holes by deriving an exact solution and examining its behavior in both near and far regions, as well as the black hole's thermodynamic properties and stability. The solution exhibits a Kerr-like structure in near regions and a Schwarzschild-like structure in far regions, with the former exhibiting rotational effects and the latter representing the nonrotating black hole in general relativity. The solution also shows a logarithmic behavior in certain functions, specifically the mass parameter $b$ and temperature parameter $T$, which are functions of the black hole's mass and the cosmological constant. The study also examines the stability of these rotating black holes using the first law of thermodynamics, which reveals that the black holes satisfy a specific condition in a certain temperature range and are stable in a range of temperatures. The research also explores the black holes' thermodynamic properties, specifically the heat capacity and the first-order phase transition, which is confirmed by the first law of thermodynamics. Numerous astrophysical processes can be represented in two-dimensional cylindrical coordinates due to their inherent symmetry. Implementing cylindrical coordinates in numerical simulations is a complex task, requiring special attention at the axis. Our research focuses on developing a highly efficient and accurate algorithm for the specific rotation and gradient operators in three-dimensional cylindrical coordinates. By utilizing this algorithm, we have created a two-dimensional solver that can be easily expanded to three-dimensional axes. Our results show that this method achieves second-order accuracy in axis-angled space and infinite accuracy at the axis. The performance of our algorithm is demonstrated using a three-dimensional MHD test case simulation.

The decays of the $D^{(*)+}_{sJ}$ mesons are observed through their reactions with $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$ and $D^{*0} K^+$. The research reveals that the $D_{sJ}^{(*)+}$ mesons primarily consist of the $D_{s}^{*}(2060)^+$ and $D_{sJ}(2860)^+$ states. The $D_{sJ}^{(*)+}$ mesons' branching ratios for these decay modes are estimated, and their properties are analyzed based on the obtained results.

This paper investigates the best polynomial approximations on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket, 
building upon a fundamental theorem that characterizes the best polynomial approximations 
on self-similar sets with uniformly bounded structure. By this theorem, the best polynomial 
approximations on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket are fractal polynomials that form an algebraic basis. 
By extending this concept, the paper further proves that fractal polynomials of a certain degree 
form the best polynomial approximations on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket, also showing that a set of 
fractal polynomials of a certain degree is sufficient to achieve the best polynomial approximations.

Traditional Visual Question Generation models generate questions based on a
single input image but our approach, Guiding Visual Question Generation, leverages
the questions of relevant, analogous scenes to aid in generating a question for a
given image. We introduce two Guiding VQG models based on transformer architectures,
which utilize multilingual capabilities. The first model utilizes image-text
descriptions to guide both the question generation and answer retrieval. The second
model employs a single model to simultaneously predict both the guiding question
and the answer. We evaluate our approach on two benchmark datasets, VQA-v2 and
Trec-VQA, and our results indicate that the proposed models significantly outperform
a single-image VQG model and rival a multi-image VQG model on these datasets.

We have developed a semi-analytical model to study the impact of supernova feedback on dark matter in dwarf galaxies. The model simulates the evolution of these galaxies over a period of 1-10 billion years, during which they experience a series of supernova explosions. We have found that the rate of energy released by supernovae influences the formation of a central core of dark matter within the galaxy. We have also discovered that the core is dissolved by subsequent supernovae explosions, which occur after a period of a few billion years. However, multiple supernova events can prevent the core dissipation, leading to a stable core formation. We have identified the conditions necessary for this phenomenon to occur, which are consistent with the observed characteristics of dwarf galaxies. Our model also explains the relationship between the mass of dark matter and the mass of stars in these galaxies. We have found that the mass of dark matter is influenced by the mass of stars, the rate of supernova feedback, and the rate of star formation.

This paper presents a set of methods for optimizing truth values and their applications in higher-order logic, and implements them within the PreProGoL preprocessing tool. We outline the major algorithmic components, demonstrate their functionality on a selection of test cases, and explain how they enhance automated theorem provers or satisfiability solvers. Furthermore, we assess the effectiveness of these methods in practice.

Research on replicator equations has revealed cycles of two-step periods in zero-sum games and more complex rotation dynamics in the set of strictly mixed equilibria. This paper explores the dynamics of zero-transposition replicator equations, which exhibit symmetries preventing the existence of cycles. However, numerical analysis and theoretical evidence indicate that these equations have an infinite number of unique, distinct patterns, including 8, 14, and 20 distinct patterns, and these patterns share a common characteristic where each cycle is followed by another cycle of the same length but opposite direction.

Random forests have been widely used for predicting outcomes and making forecasts. However, their probabilistic nature in predictions remains underutilized. Research has been done to address this issue, and a recent study proposes a new method to create a random forest confidence distribution. The proposed method is a non-parametric approach that considers the forest's trees as independent paths. It provides a closed-form expression for the density and allows for the computation of the distribution at any point. Additionally, its asymptotic properties are derived. The method was tested on both real-world and simulated datasets, and the results showed its effectiveness in capturing the underlying distributional nature of the data.

This study examines the potential impact of electric vehicle charging and discharging on local grid voltages and the battery energy system's performance when optimal coordination is absent. In a case study involving a high-resolution, real-world network, it was found that the battery's life span is reduced by up to 9% when its operation is not synchronized with the grid voltages in a specific network. A new control method is proposed that aligns charging and discharging times with local grid voltages, resulting in reduced peak to valley ratios and improved coordination between charging and discharging. Compared to a conventional method, this approach achieves a 1.5% improvement in battery life span and a 0.5% increase in charging capacity at a 30-minute state of charge depth.

This research focuses on the structural characteristics of samarium orthoferrite (SmOF), a material with potential superconducting properties, particularly at high pressures. By examining SmF$_3$ and FeO$_3$ phase diagrams under pressure, it's discovered that SmOF can be synthesized at lower pressures than SmFe$_3$O$_5$ synthesis requirements. Using first-principles calculations, it's determined that SmOF's stability is influenced by pressure, leading to a transition from monoclinic to orthorhombic structures. Analysis of the electronic and phonon properties reveals that the orthorhombic structure is stable at pressures above 30 GPa, while monoclinic and low-pressure orthorhombic structures are unstable. These high-pressure phases also show no superconductivity. However, at 40 GPa, SmOF's electronic structure changes, leading to a potential superconducting state, characterized by the appearance of Sm 4f conduction electrons, suggesting that doping SmOF with Sm can create superconductivity.

In ecology, the application of Cumulative Effectiveness is crucial for assessing the persistence of species and the impact on the environment over time. However, a major challenge is that current methods require extensive data collection, limiting their potential application in real-time scenarios. We propose a new approach that uses a combination of machine learning and time-series analysis to accurately calculate Cumulative Effectiveness in real-time, even with minimal data available. Our results show that this method can effectively estimate Cumulative Effectiveness and provide reliable results, even with as little as 2 data points. This new approach has the potential to revolutionize the application of Cumulative Effectiveness by enabling its real-time assessment across diverse ecosystems.

To address the issue of missing fundamental and mass balance equations in ventilation systems, a method of modeling these systems is developed, focusing on accurately reproducing airflow measurements. The method, a form of black-box modeling, uses data from low-lying, submerged air intakes and outlets collected over a 10-second interval. Univariate and multivariate time series autoregressive models are applied to individual air intake and outlet dynamic behavior to identify key factors influencing airflow, and the predictive accuracy of the models is evaluated. The time series models effectively replicated airflow in intakes and outlets, with the multivariate approach achieving the best results for air outlet prediction and moderate accuracy for an air intake. The models provide fundamental insights and mass balance equations for ventilation systems, allowing for system identification and control design.

We have analyzed the light-curve and spectral characteristics of a one-year-old supernova in NGC 2778 using the Gemini/GMOS spectroscopic and CANDELS/HST imaging data. The results of our investigation suggest that the supernova in NGC 2778 exhibits characteristics similar to those of a hydrogen-poor superluminous supernova (SLSN), featuring a rapid rise in brightness, a peak luminosity of $10^{44.5-44.6}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, and a unique spectral profile. Notably, the supernova in question appears to be underluminous compared to other SLSNe, and its spectrum does not match that of any other SLSN. Our findings indicate that the supernova in NGC 2778 is likely a SLSN, and its unique spectral signature may be attributed to the interaction between the supernova ejecta and the circumstellar medium.

Our research delves into the thermodynamic behavior of planar magnetic systems
with a specific geometric arrangement, and reveals a significant distinction
between 2D and 3D magnetic properties. The existence of a unique temperature
threshold separates these two regimes and is characterized by a distinct
pattern of spin fluctuations. The findings indicate that the hysteresis
curve of a planar magnetic system will exhibit unique asymmetry, reflecting
the system's inherent geometry-dependent characteristics.

Our investigation focuses on the effect of word image associations on the development of grammar rules for parsing sentences. We hypothesize that word concreteness plays a significant role in the learning process, given its importance in understanding relationships between objects in the physical world. To explore this connection, we suggest that similar comprehension abilities for abstract relationships require a similar foundation in concrete understanding. We have adapted the PARSE-MIND system to incorporate visual word representations, replacing its original text-only inputs with a combination of text and images. Evaluating its performance on the Penn Treebank corpus against a control model using solely textual data reveals a notable enhancement in grammar learning and robustness, particularly in handling obscure terms and out-of-vocabulary words.

Attribution map evaluation methods evaluate how accurate an attribution map is in relation to the true activation map.  A new method of attribution map evaluation is introduced in this paper.  The proposed method requires no ground truth data and relies on a random mask generator to simulate different scenarios.  The effectiveness of the new method is tested using various types of images and image classification models trained with diverse techniques, and it is found that common benchmarks may be flawed in assessing various types of attribution maps.  The proposed method can be used to compare different attribution map methods under real-world conditions.  The method can be used to train models that produce more accurate attribution maps by incorporating a novel loss function.  The method can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of different models in various tasks.  The method can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of the new method by comparing it to other existing methods.

Researchers have discovered a new class of black holes, specifically thin-shell wormholes, that exhibit reflection asymmetry and are stable across wide mass ratios when endow with negative cosmological constant, appearing as a new type of four-dimensional rotating Morris-Thorne wormhole. The study of these wormholes, labeled MThR, has revealed an unusual energy condition and some distinct features, such as the absence of event horizons and unique gravitational behavior, as well as a potential for invariable throat radius when embedded in the Schwarzschild-Dirac metric. Furthermore, the exploration of MThR in the context of the Kerr-Schild metric has facilitated the derivation of its rotation function and some interesting properties, such as the equivalence to a Schwarzschild wormhole in the static limit and the presence of a unique ergosurface. The study of these wormholes, which also exhibit a bond between mass and radius, has raised the possibility of their detection through gravitational waves.

We have derived a novel functional inequality applicable to correlated multi-particle processes, which effectively subsumes extended versions of previous inequalities. Notably, this new inequality surpasses the extended Greenberg-Hastings inequality for both uncorrelated and correlated systems. Furthermore, our findings yield sharp lower bounds for the rate-fidelity deviation in single and multiple qubit systems, which align with previously derived limits under independent states.

Researchers have been studying trimer covers, a type of graph theory model, on triangular lattices for nearly 40 years. A recent work by Gurevich and Shelah provided significant insight into the uniqueness of such configurations. The focus of our paper lies in examining the properties of these triangular trimer covers, specifically their relationship to another well-studied lattice model known as planar spin lattice formulas, where recent breakthroughs were achieved by Bishop and Zmijewski.

Domain adaptation, particularly the universal type which caters to distributional shifts in source and target domains, is a key area of research in NLP. However, current state-of-the-art UDA methods rely heavily on expensive, large-scale pretraining. This work presents an efficient, transfer learning-based framework for UDA that is cost-effective and effective. It uses a multilingual BERT model and adapts the target domain in a step-by-step manner, initially learning domain-invariant representations through unsupervised training and subsequently fine-tuning the model under target tasks. Experimental results on NLU and NLP datasets demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses the performance of pretraining-based UDA methods, while also being more economical.

The process of 3D reconstruction from 2D images is enhanced when prior object knowledge is incorporated, as it enables the identification of unique shapes in an image based on known object models. This approach is particularly useful in scenarios where direct 3D reconstruction is not feasible due to occlusions or limited viewpoints. This research presents a method that utilizes a hierarchical 3D-2D part correspondence for 3D object reconstruction, where the topmost layer incorporates object size and center position prior knowledge, while the second layer learns size-independent features from a single object model. The approach is demonstrated to be effective through its application in 3D pose and shape reconstruction from real-world images, specifically in the context of chair reconstruction.

The Query Graph Ranking (QGR) model has been successful in answering complex questions by using a structured query over a knowledge base, responding naturally. However, recent experiments have shown that neural network-based QGR models struggle with common language challenges such as parsing, reasoning, and handling ambiguous questions. This paper proposes an enhanced QGR model that incorporates a pre-trained structure predictor to ensure the generated query graph accurately represents the intended structure from the natural language question. We also introduce a pre-trained function learner to improve the scoring function, allowing it to better account for complex relationships and non-standard query functions. By combining these improvements, we create a robust QGR model that surpasses state-of-the-art performance on complex question benchmark datasets.

This paper introduces the concepts of polynomial composites and establishes their connection to fundamental algebraic properties. It examines how these composites interact with Galois theory, Kronecker product, and other underlying principles. Furthermore, polynomials with rational or matrix entries are used to illustrate their applications.

The process of identifying named entities and disambiguating them is a critical task in natural language processing.  However, current approaches often fail to address the complexity of NED, which is plagued by issues such as ambiguity and context dependency.  Existing methods often rely on limited information sources, such as Wikipedia, and struggle to handle the vast number of named entities appearing in the real world.  In order to address these limitations, this study proposes a novel framework that leverages the knowledge graph embedded in the Structured Knowledge (SK) and utilizes the Graph Neural Network (GNN) to learn the vector representations of entities from their graph structures.  By incorporating multiple knowledge sources, SK can effectively capture the semantic meanings of entities and their relationships, and the GNN framework allows the model to incorporate the structural information of named entities and improve its performance.  Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in handling NED tasks.

In this work, we have determined the one-loop oblique corrections to $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), taking into consideration gaugino mass unification. Our calculations were performed at the one-loop level and to next-to-next-to-leading order in the top Yukawa coupling within the on-shell renormalization scheme. Our findings have been applied to a global fit of electroweak precision data, yielding results consistent with previous research. In particular, we have identified a next-to-next-to-leading order contribution to $S$ that had not been accounted for in past studies.

We propose an algorithm for producing novel perspectives based on a single video of an active scene environment. Our method combines the benefits of learning-based approaches with traditional geometric techniques to achieve more realistic results. It starts by creating a 3D model of the environment and then uses this representation to generate novel views of the scene. Our approach is unique in that it can adapt to changing lighting conditions and requires no additional training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in producing high-quality novel views from a publicly available dataset. Our project is planned for release as an open-source tool, allowing for further research into this topic.

This research paper investigates a type of rough differential equation with a complex stabilising force. Although this damping factor isn't affiliated with any specific group, it does have an infinitesimal dilation symmetry. The properties of this symmetry play a significant role in the research and its findings. The primary focus of the study is to establish the global asymptotic stability of certain linear RDEs, building on the previous work of Chaudhuri, and even surpassing it by offering more robust conclusions.

We suggest a two-dimensional random grain model that exhibits dependence over long distances. This model is based on a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$, where each point is associated with an isotropic random sector of angle $\theta \in (0,\pi)$.  We establish that the random grain density $f(x)$ is solved from the equation $ \int_0^{\pi} e^{i\theta \tan \theta} e^{-i\theta^* x} d\theta = \lambda f(x)$.  We prove that the random grain density has a Fourier transform of the form $\hat{f}(u) = \lambda e^{|u| / \lambda}$ for $|u|$ large, and that the random grain process is strongly mixing with a mixing rate going to zero as the grain size increases.  This process is strongly mixing with a mixing rate going to zero as the grain size increases.  This result is achieved by showing that the random grain process is a realization of a Poisson random measure with a covariance operator of the form $S_0 + S_1(|u|)$ where $S_0$ is a constant times the identity operator and $S_1(|u|)$ is a kernel of the form $c_1 |u|^{-\alpha_1}$ with $c_1, \alpha_1$ satisfying certain conditions.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) have the potential to significantly enhance the capabilities of the next generation of wireless networks. In order to effectively integrate RISs into future networks, it is essential to thoroughly understand the impact of these devices on the underlying physics and system performance. This research paper provides an in-depth analysis of the benefits offered by RISs in various scenarios, with a focus on three distinct cases: (i) single-user transmission, (ii) non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) with a single user, and (iii) NOMA with multiple concurrent users. The results of our analysis reveal the advantages offered by RISs, as well as the limitations imposed by practical considerations such as hardware limitations, environmental factors, and interference. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights that can guide future research into the applications of RISs in wireless networks.

This research focuses on developing probabilistic solutions to complex equations using the deep RNN learning approach, particularly for multi-agent systems influenced by random factors. The authors apply a large deviation theory to create an extended dynamic model that incorporates path integrals to represent these random effects. The resulting deep learning method is then applied to solve the mean-field optimal control problem, demonstrating its effectiveness through numerical simulations which also reveal the impact of stochastic noise on control strategies.

A new method of quantization-aware training has been developed to fine-tune the weights of convolutional neural networks, reducing their bit depth from 32-bit to 1-bit weights while maintaining performance. This approach involves a two-stage training process where the network is first trained in its original form, with 32-bit weights, before being subject to a bit-restricted quantization of its weights. This method significantly improves performance compared to traditional training methods, specifically yielding a top-1 accuracy of 68.0% on the CIFAR-10 dataset when compared to the ResNet-20 model in ImageNet, while also outperforming other methods on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.

The phenomenon of Type Ia supernovae, which result from the explosion of white dwarf stars, continues to fascinate scientists with its intricacies. Research into the causes of these explosions continues to produce intriguing findings, including multiple mechanisms and various configurations. Recent studies have shed light on diverse scenarios that can lead to an explosive white dwarf. This paper reviews the current understanding of CSM accretion onto white dwarims, which was initially proposed as a type of delayed thermonuclear explosion mechanism. The study specifically examines the process of CSM accretion onto white dwarims, its impact on thermonuclear ignition, and how it relates to diverse configurations. The paper also discusses the significance of CSM accretion in the context of Type Ia supernovae, its potential to produce diverse observational features, and how it relates to other supernova phenomena.

Recent studies have shown that online learning with deep neural networks can be made sample-efficient by adjusting the trade-off between computing power and sample availability in line with the data's difficulty level. However, these findings rely on theoretical assumptions and are not applicable to practical scenarios where the difficulty level of incoming data is unknown. This paper proposes a new approach to optimize the performance of deep neural networks through a dynamic allocation of computational resources based on the data's difficulty level. We establish a theoretical connection between the learning process and the optimization problem, and then develop a solution based on a new optimization technique that can be used in an online learning setting. We show that our algorithm converges to the best policy and we also provide a practical implementation that can be used in real-world applications. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in various online learning tasks, such as image classification on ImageNet and medical diagnosis on a large clinical dataset.

The emergence of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has led to the COVID-19 pandemic, causing millions of cases worldwide, with hundreds of thousands of fatalities.  In an effort to curb the virus's spread, governments have implemented strict lockdowns, and researchers have been striving to develop effective vaccines and treatments since the beginning of 2020.  Unfortunately, COVID-19-related vaccines have not been entirely successful in preventing infection or transmitting the disease.  In an attempt to ensure public safety, many countries have introduced strict lockdowns, limiting travel and introducing strict testing and vaccination protocols.  In an effort to address these challenges, we propose a blockchain-based solution to enable individuals to securely manage their COVID-19 testing and vaccination records.  Our proposed system allows users to create digital wallets that can be updated in real-time, reflecting their current vaccination status.  In an attempt to prevent individuals from misrepresenting their vaccination status, we propose a blockchain-based system that rewards honest individuals with bonus tokens, while penalizing those who provide false information.  Our proposed system is designed to be user-friendly, requiring only a few steps to claim rewards after providing a positive COVID-19 test result.  In an effort to minimize the impact of self-reported data on blockchain transactions, we propose a solution that utilizes a secure digital storage system, with a human auditing mechanism in place to verify the accuracy of such transactions.  Our proposed system is designed to be highly scalable, and user-friendly, with a digital

This paper presents an in-depth analysis of sentence embedding models, comparing their pre-trained representations in a supervised task – specifically, the classification of sentences into distinct categories. Our goal is to identify the most effective models and hyperparameter combinations for this task, without relying on extensive new data. Through a comprehensive hyperparameter search using AutoML techniques, we evaluate the performance of four popular sentence embedding models, leveraging a large dataset of product descriptions. By applying these models to this dataset, we achieve state-of-the-art results in zero-shot text classification across 47 product categories, surpassing existing benchmarks.

We investigate the diffusion of quantum particles on a $d$-dimensional lattice, focusing on how the diffusion changes when we either add or remove particle-hole symmetry. To do this, we use a combination of real-space renormalization group and perturbation theory to understand the differences in diffusion when this symmetry is preserved or broken, quantifying these differences through various parameters. Furthermore, we derive an expression that relates the diffusion of a system without particle-hole symmetry to the diffusion of a system with it, allowing us to calculate the diffusion coefficient in both cases using a perturbative approach.

In a quantum Hall ferromagnet, the Kerr precession is triggered by a variation in the orientation of the ground state, resulting in the precession of a spin wave. The attenuation of this precession is caused by the decay of the spin wave itself, the interaction with electron continuum states, or Landau damping. We find that Landau damping significantly shortens the precession time, making it comparable to the time it takes for the ground state to return to equilibrium. Furthermore, we propose a method to measure the Landau damping rate of a quantum Hall ferromagnet by utilizing the precession of the ground state near a quantum Hall edge.

We investigated the behavior of a conformal field theory under periodic driving conditions, focusing on its distinct phases and the critical boundary separating them. Our research revealed that in this setup, the driven theory exhibits two main phases: a regime of weak driving where the system behaves like an undriven system and a highly driven regime where it displays periodic oscillations. Through a combination of analytical and numerical approaches, we identified and analyzed the critical fixed point, leveraging the concept of effective temperatures to derive scaling dimensions and investigating their dependence on the driving period.

A novel, advanced deep learning model is developed for fusing data from multiple sources in sensor-based systems. This model can learn to represent combined sensory information in an unsupervised manner and generate missing data from available sensory inputs. Our proposed model utilizes a variational autoencoder framework to achieve these goals. By incorporating multiple autoencoders and a corresponding latent variable, it acquires knowledge of sensory representations and their interdependencies. A classifier is then trained on these latent variables to produce a unified representation. In experiments involving a real-world dataset from a visual-inertial sensor platform, our model demonstrated the ability to accurately forecast missing data and successfully complete a SLAM task.

The $C\!P$-violating phase in the mixing-induced $C\!P$ violation of $D^0$-$\bar D^0$ and $B^0$-$\bar B^0$ systems is a crucial element in the Standard Model that can help resolve the $B^0$-$\bar B^0$ system's value. This phase, denoted by $\phi_D$, can be measured through the decay rates of $D^0$ to $K_S^0\pi^+\pi^-$, with the use of super-strong $C\!P$ violation in $K_S^0$ decay. By employing a machine learning technique, this phase can be determined from the decay rates of $D^0$ to various final states. This study presents a measurement of the $\phi_D$ phase using the $D^0$-$K_S^0\pi^+\pi^-$-$K_S^0$ system, with the data collected by the Belle II detector. By analyzing the data collected from an integrated luminosity of $62.8$ fb$^{-1}$, this phase is found to be within the range of $-0.25\pi^2$ to $0.10\pi^2$ with the confidence level of 68.8%.

This paper presents a new class of optimization problems known as Graph Symmetric Systems, for which optimal control strategies can be directly applied through a compact representation that remains consistent with the problem's continuous counterpart. This representation is further enhanced with the introduction of a novel distributed optimal control approach, referred to as Graph Symmetric Systems with Distributed Optimal Control (GSSDOC). The proposed GSSDOC framework is characterized by a compact representation that can be mapped to a graph, with each node corresponding to a specific control variable. The framework's compact representation is also amenable to a decentralized solution, where control variables can be computed independently by individual nodes. The theoretical foundations of the proposed GSSDOC framework are rigorously established, with key findings including the convergence of the control strategy, the optimality of the compact representation, and the equivalence of the discrete-time and continuous-time frameworks. The proposed GSSDOC framework is demonstrated to be effective through a variety of case studies.

This study examines the application of labeled random finite set (RFS) representation within a Bayesian framework to track multiple objects. The labeled LRF method, known as the multi-Bernoulli random finite set filter, has inherent computational limitations, a result of increasing RFS dimension. To mitigate this issue, a modified version, the labeled random finite mixture filter, utilizes a probability of belonging to each component as a key metric. The implementation of a specific truncation criterion significantly reduces computational complexity. Theoretical analysis of the filter's convergence and variance is provided, with supporting experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of the approach.

Linguistic knowledge bases, like WALS, play a significant role in facilitating linguistic research but are limited by their low state of standardization and incompleteness. This gap in typological data poses a significant challenge to researchers looking to integrate and build upon this data. To address this issue, we created a platform that allows researchers to compile and disseminate standardized, open-source data. By utilizing this tool, we also standardized and disseminated the WALS dataset, making the process transparent and accessible. Additionally, we released a revised, standardized version of the Ethnologue, a comprehensive dictionary containing information about languages and dialects worldwide. We made public the raw data, as well as pre-trained models for 103 languages, and provided a web-based API for accessing and querying this data.

Our research focuses on addressing the off-policy evaluation challenge, which involves calculating the expected return of a learned policy from an existing dataset generated by a different policy. To achieve this, we propose a new approach called the locally generalized maximum entropy algorithm, which utilizes a novel duality theory to calculate the expected return. This approach enables us to represent the value function as a constrained version of an optimization problem, and our results show that it can handle high-dimensionality and discontinuous environments. Furthermore, we develop a novel sample-based estimator that can handle high-dimensionality and provide theoretical guarantees for its off-policy correctness. Our experiments confirm that this algorithm outperforms existing methods in various high-dimensionality and discontinuous benchmarks.

In the fermentation stage of biopharmaceutical production, accurately controlling temperature, pressure, and the concentration of nutrients and waste products is critical. However, the fermentation process is further complicated by the challenge of model risk, where existing models fail to accurately predict real-world phenomena. To address this issue, we propose a robust optimization framework that can effectively manage model risk by formulating an optimization problem with multiple possible model outcomes and their associated uncertainty levels. By leveraging this framework, we can determine robust operating conditions that are resilient to model inaccuracies. We then develop an algorithm that can efficiently solve the resulting optimization problem and validate its efficacy through a case study.
