Our analysis identified numerous accessibility issues, primarily related to the use of alternative input methods and insufficient error message provision.

The task of learning new skills from minimal data while retaining previously acquired knowledge is known as few-shot continual learning. Although this concept has been explored in the past, there is a significant gap in understanding how humans achieve this level of learning. In an attempt to bridge this knowledge gap, we propose a model of human learning that combines the idea of executive functions with machine learning's few-shot continual learning. Executive functions, a key aspect of human cognition, enable the control and adaptation of skills in response to changing circumstances. We develop a neural network model that simulates human executive functions and learns to improve its performance on new tasks with minimal data while retaining its knowledge of previous tasks. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our model can learn to improve its performance on new tasks with minimal data while retaining its knowledge of previous tasks.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning heavily relies on the quality of the available dataset, which unfortunately often suffers from biases resulting from data collection, causing any learned models to pick up and reflect these biases. As a result, any insights derived from these learned models may not be applicable in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we have developed a new method that utilizes a two-part approach to mitigate biases present in medical image datasets. This involves initially identifying and quantifying the underlying biases using a novel metric, followed by a method to remove the biases. We have also demonstrated the practicality of our approach using a real-world dataset of digital pathology images.

Despite the success of metric learning in real-world applications, its performance is often hampered by the prevalence of noisy labels. A new approach to address this issue is presented in the paper, which combines metric learning with a robust loss function that can learn to tolerate label errors. The proposed method, called Robust Metric Learning, employs a two-stage training process that can be viewed as learning a distribution of optimal metric models. In the first stage, an initial metric model is trained using a robust loss function, and the second stage involves sampling and fine-tuning this model. Experimental results demonstrate that RML significantly outperforms existing noise-robust metric learning methods across multiple benchmark datasets.

Investigating the cosmological information contained in N-point statistics is crucial for achieving a deeper understanding of the universe, yet it is still a developing area of research. We developed a new and efficient estimator based on the Minimum Variance Unbiasing Certainty Equivalent Estimator to gauge higher-order N-point statistics. Our analysis, conducted within the framework of the CosmoFlow framework, involved simulating the statistical properties of 2D power spectra and higher-order 2-point correlations. Our results show that the estimator is accurate to a 1% margin for up to 6-order correlations and 2-point correlations. Our findings indicate that the estimated higher-order N-point statistics are consistent with the true values, demonstrating the estimator's efficacy in cosmological applications.

We investigate the fractionalized excitation spectrum of an SO(5) non-Abelian spinor Bose liquid with a U(1) symmetry in an SO(5) representation using the Schwinger boson model. By employing a mean-field analysis, we derive a quantum phase diagram featuring an emergent SO(5) superfluid with topological features, a superfluid with partially broken SO(5) symmetry, and a paramagnetic phase. The SO(5) superfluid exhibits a rich topological quantum structure, characterized by a non-trivial correlation function and a 5D representation in the momentum space, as well as a 5D Chern number and a non-zero Berry phase. The SO(5) superfluid also displays a non-zero topological Hall effect and a non-zero Berry phase. The SO(5) superfluid is a non-trivial topological superfluid with a non-zero topological Hall effect and a non-zero Berry phase.

Micropixel avalanche photodiodes (MAPDs) offer a combination of high sensitivity, low power consumption, and small pixel size, making them suitable for use in scintillation detectors. This study investigates the performance of MAPDs in detecting scintillation light from LaBr$_3$, Ce:$(LiF,Mg)_2SiO$_4)$, and $LiGdAsO$_4$, as well as the performance of MAPDs in single-photoelectron detection at various anode voltages. The study also examines the linear gain of MAPDs in response to anode voltage changes.

This study examines how the characteristics of ideal behavior in a local ring change when its elements are multiplied by positive real numbers. The investigation specifically focuses on equations that define Cohen-Macaulay local rings, especially those related to Ehrhart series and special rings, such as Betti, Serre, and Gorenstein rings. It also explores the behavior of minimal and weakly Stanley-Reisner ideals under this transformation.

Our research focuses on the magnetic and transport properties of the compound Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) under high-pressure conditions, specifically within a range of 0 to 40 GPa.  The compound exhibits a complex magnetic structure with interlinked ferro-magnetic and anti-ferro-magnetic axes at room temperature.  As pressure increases, the magnetic ordering transitions from ordered to disordered to ordered again, with the disordered phase showing anti-ferro-magnetic characteristics at low temperatures.  The application of pressure also leads to a significant increase in the magnetocaloric effect in the ordered phase, with the maximum entropy change rising to 21.8 J/kg·K at 4.5 GPa, which is higher than the room temperature value.  The compound's behavior is also influenced by the spin reorientation pressure, which is estimated to be around 30 GPa.

This paper presents a novel approach to designing a versatile trading strategy, which can be tailored to match the distribution of a custom benchmark as it evolves over time. Our goal is to ensure that the deviations of the portfolio from the benchmark are limited and conform to the normal distribution for any specified time period. The proposed method incorporates multiple parameters that can be adjusted to suit various scenarios. Our statistical technique is tested and validated using simulated data with artificially generated returns based on the normal distribution, as well as real-world market data obtained from the EDHEC Risk Institute. The results show that our strategy effectively converges to the target distribution after a relatively short period, typically 30 to 40 months. Moreover, the strategy successfully manages to reduce the frequency and intensity of extreme market fluctuations, which are often characterized by fat tails in financial distributions.

A tunable add-drop filter based on a double-disk cavity optomechanical system is developed, featuring a broad tuning range of 30 nm and 100 pm, as well as a 0.2% droop efficiency. This efficiency is enhanced by the precise alignment of optical and mechanical modes, enabled by the rigid mechanical disk. The operation of the filter is influenced by the mechanical mode coupling with the optical mode, resulting in a resonant reflection peak within the cavity resonance band. Furthermore, the filter's performance is improved by the optomechanical effect, which is strong and stable due to the double-disk structure and the optomechanical interaction between the mechanical and optical modes.

Public health officials can utilize online activity to gauge the effectiveness of public health measures, and social media platforms like Twitter play a vital role in this process. This paper presents a method to quantify the impact of physical distancing measures through the analysis of tweet interactions, specifically those indicative of in-person contact. Our approach employs a dual strategy to estimate the number of in-person interactions: first, identifying potential encounters between individuals and then calculating the likelihood of actual contact. Our findings are demonstrated using data collected from London during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In several image compression benchmarks, the recommended data transfer rate falls short of the minimum required for various practical applications like image recognition and transmission over networks. This discrepancy becomes more pronounced when working with larger image dimensions, leading to a notable delay in between the ideal speed (ranging from 1,000 to 100,000 pixels per second) and the actual speed achievable using existing neural network-based compression tools (ranging from 10 to 1,000 pixels per second). To address this issue, we developed a novel network called OptFlow that efficiently handles high-speed image compression by utilizing a hierarchical approach, thereby minimizing the search area for motion estimation and reducing the number of computations needed. This approach is further optimized through the use of a unique entropy coding technique that exploits the inherent redundancy in the multiple layers of the motion field. Experimental results demonstrate that OptFlow achieves a balance between high-quality images (with PSNR values exceeding 30 dB) and exceptional speed (transmitting 192x192 images at 100,000 pixels per second).

Using 4.08 fb^-1 of data collected from proton-proton collisions at the LHCb, researchers have conducted a detailed analysis of the B+ to D_s+ K+K- decay. They have measured the branching fraction of this process to be (23.1 ± 5.0 ± 1.3) × 10^-4, with the first uncertainty being statistical and the second systematic. Furthermore, they have identified several Ds(*) spin-parity states with varying levels of certainty, specifically Ds(2^+), Ds(2*-), Ds(3^-), and Ds(1^-), with the former two being relatively well established and the latter having moderate evidence. In addition, they have discovered the first observation of Ds(3^-) with a spin parity J^P = 3^- in the B+ to D_s+ K+K- decay, with a significance of 5.3 standard deviations.

In machine learning, the combination of optimal transport and robust statistics has been a successful blend, thanks to its robustness to outliers. Despite this, the most commonly used OT loss functions in ML, such as M-OT and Sinkhorn distance, exhibit problematic behavior when dealing with outliers. Specifically, they can produce arbitrarily large gradients in response to outliers, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we've introduced a new class of differentiable and semiparametrically efficient OT loss functions, referred to as Huber OT loss. By substituting the traditional Euclidean norm in OT with the more robust Huber norm, our proposed solution effectively guards against outliers. Our experiments demonstrate that the Huber OT loss functions outperform existing alternatives in real-world scenarios.

The development of artificial intelligence that can collaborate with humans in competitive situations remains an unresolved challenge. We address this issue by creating AI agents capable of playing the strategic card game Hanabi under constraints of time and resources. We experiment with human-AI collaborations in a simulated setting, where we also explore the feasibility of a human introducing modifications to the game's rules.

The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012 at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, is of great interest to physicists. Researchers are now seeking to understand the fundamental nature of the Standard Model and its potential flaws. A key area of focus involves supersymmetry, a concept that suggests the existence of companion particles to the Standard Model's fermions and scalars, which could explain the Higgs boson's low mass. A new study examines the impact of supersymmetric particles on the Higgs boson's properties, focusing on its decay patterns and the production processes that occur in a background-free environment. The research also explores how these effects vary with the Higgs boson's mass and the supersymmetric particles' coupling strength. Additionally, the study examines the potential constraints on supersymmetry imposed by the Higgs boson's observed characteristics.

This study delves into how cognitive skills and linguistic proficiency influence people's ability to comprehend and interpret intricate visual data representations. We examine how individual mental abilities, like spatial awareness, and language skills impact people's performance when using these complex visualizations. We also compare the capabilities of professionals with diverse expertise in spatial reasoning and language skills to see if their experience in communicating and interpreting data gives them an advantage. We discovered that people's cognitive skills and language proficiency are crucial in determining their ability to understand and analyze intricate visual data. Moreover, our results suggest that experts with extensive experience in processing and interpreting spatially complex data have an advantage over non-experts, regardless of their language proficiency.

This research examines the algorithmic proof of cyclic sets of clauses using automated reasoning tools. We establish an algorithmic method for finding an induction scheme for cyclic sets based on a modified version of the concept of harmonic division. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an induced induction scheme for a cycle in theory $\forall 1$ is sufficient to induce a scheme within the same theory. Additionally, we provide an explanation of the reasons behind the chosen harmonic division definition and suggest directions for future research, focusing on generalizing the concept to other theories and evaluating the efficiency of the induced induction scheme.

Recent advancements in neural networks have led to significant improvements in graph retrieval, with focus on graph classification, clustering, and anomaly detection. This research provides a comprehensive overview of neural networks-based approaches for graph retrieval, covering recent developments in graph representation learning, particularly neural networks that utilize subgraph sampling and aggregation techniques to achieve effective graph retrieval. We examine the use of these methods for predicting graph labels, identifying cluster groups, and detecting graph anomalies. Finally, we discuss the challenges and potential future research directions in this field.

Recent advancements in machine learning techniques and the proliferation of big data have greatly enhanced the capabilities of computer vision algorithms. However, the field of computer vision still faces challenges in extracting data from images with complex backgrounds, dealing with missing data, and analyzing data in detail. To address these issues, researchers are leveraging the latest natural language processing techniques, including semantic analysis and neural networks, to improve computer vision and extract more information from images. This study examines the current state of research in image-text pairing and explores how semantic analysis can inform computer vision algorithms, leading to a greater understanding of image meaning and improved accuracy in tasks like image recognition and classification.

In countries where electricity generation falls short of demand, a standard solution to the imbalance involves disconnecting certain loads to maintain supply equilibrium. This practice of load shedding poses a significant challenge to those households in need of electricity, particularly those with higher requirements. To mitigate this issue, a more equitable allocation of electricity supply can be achieved by selectively disconnecting loads in a targeted manner. This research presents a model that enables utilities to identify the loads most suitable for disconnection, thus minimizing the resulting inconvenience and social impact. This model relies on survey data to estimate the probability of a household experiencing difficulties in meeting its basic electricity requirements. Once a load shedding decision is made, utilities can determine which specific loads to disconnect, thus maximizing social welfare. This research provides empirical evidence from Pakistan to validate the model's effectiveness.

The challenge of event coreference resolution involves determining which pairs of relevant events are linked or unrelated within a given corpus. Previous approaches have focused on either hand-crafted features or representation learning, but these methods have limitations when dealing with large, complex datasets. To address this, we propose a new framework that combines a transformer encoder with an attention mechanism to improve the accuracy of event coreference. We also introduce a new, refined evaluation metric that better captures the complexities of event coreference, and we utilize this metric to assess our approach, comparing it to existing methods. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms previous approaches, achieving a new benchmark in performance.

The Complementarity Knapsack Problem, a more challenging variant of the traditional knapsack issue, involves items with conflicting benefits and costs within limited capacity. In this extended version, multiple knapsacks with the capability to use simultaneous processing are explored. It is essential to acknowledge that solving this problem is computationally complex, specifically NP-hard. Various optimization methods have been developed to tackle its complexity, including exact methods, heuristics, and metaheurics. A novel hybrid approach, a combination of the Variable Neighborhood Search and Random Walk, is introduced to find a more efficient solution for this problem. The proposed method's performance is compared with other existing solutions for its variants on diverse datasets.

This paper delves into the potential loss of idempotency for the product of two generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations that add up to a generalized $(m,n)$-derivation. Our investigation focuses on a semiprime ring and reveals the consequences of our findings are also applicable to prime rings and also hold true for the specific case of derivations. Our results indicate that in these particular cases, the idempotency of the sum is equivalent to the idempotency of the original derivation, a generalized Jordan derivation, and the derivate in question.

In our study, we examine the structure of high-energy scattering amplitudes by analyzing the low-energy behavior and applying the inverse scattering method to transform the low to high energy process. This is achieved through the factorization of low to high energy amplitudes, where the low-energy terms are represented by the inverse scattering method, and the high-energy terms are described by the 1/N expansion. Our research focuses on the specific case of a coupled channel scattering system that includes an infinite number of channels. The model we developed is a 1+1 dimensional relativistic field theory with a real scalar field that exhibits a non-trivial infrared behavior. The model consists of two channels with two and one relevant operators, and it is solvable in the low-energy regime. By using the inverse scattering method, we generated an analytic solution for the model, and by extending this solution, we were able to describe the system with an infinite number of channels. The solution also allows us to describe the system in the high-energy regime, and by analyzing the solution, we found that it exhibits a 1/N expansion. The solution also shows that the conformal dimensions of the operators in the model, and the velocities of the solitons, are related to the coupling constants of the model, and that the solution also shows the existence of a soliton-antisoliton bound state. We investigate the asymptotic behavior of nonlinear generalizations of the Favard length in the context of two-dimensional polynomial fibrations over a unit disk. Our study reveals that the rate of decay for these nonlinear variants of the Favard length is characterized by logarithmic terms. This leads to a natural question: what is the minimal degree of a polynomial that induces a Favard length decaying at a $\log\log{|z|}|x|^2$ rate for large $|z|$? We demonstrate that the degree of the polynomial can be arbitrarily high, even if it favors one direction over the other. However, if both directions exhibit the same decay behavior, then the degree of the polynomial is strictly below four.

Autonomous systems face uncertainty in the form of external disturbances, which can be unpredictable and changeable in non-linear systems. Consequently, it's difficult to ensure that a system will reach its desired target despite these uncertainties. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a Robust Tube variant of Model Predictive Control, which provides a guarantee that a system will reach its target even when faced with uncertain disturbances. To achieve this, we create a set of possible system paths that ensures at least one path will successfully reach the target, making our approach more reliable than previous uncertainty-based control methods. Our approach is tested in a simulation of an autonomous racing car and on a system observing a linear quadratic regulator.

In a specific type of antiferromagnet, we investigate the anomalous Hall effect when magnetic field strength is extremely low. Under these conditions, the magnetic structure remains unchanged but an unusual kind of current emerges due to a rare and unique phenomenon related to Berry curvature. By analyzing a particular material modelled after the spin-polarized p-d band ferromagnet known as Mn$_3X$, we calculate the effect of this curvature on transport properties across a range of parameters including coupling strength, spin-orbit interaction and chemical potential. Our findings suggest that this effect can significantly impact transport behavior when magnetic fields are weak. While we find that this effect can be small compared to other effects such as Hall and ordinary Berry curvatures, we observe that it may become dominant when magnetic field strength reaches a few Tesla. Furthermore, the effect can be further enhanced by a specific type of interaction between magnetic fields and material boundaries. Our study provides new insights into the anomalous Hall effect when magnetic fields are weak and highlights the importance of understanding the intricate interplay between material structure, the magnetic field and the resulting current.

Researchers use object-oriented programming languages in various scientific fields, 
utilizing parallel libraries to perform significant tasks. To understand performance 
issues and optimize these systems, analyzing the call graph is essential, but manual 
analysis becomes impractical with increasing program size and complexity. To address 
this challenge, we propose ensemble-Sankey, a visualization method that uses 
interactive call graphs. Unlike traditional Sankey, ensemble-Sankey visualizes multiple 
pathways through the call graph, making it easier to identify various call flow 
patterns. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we conducted a user study 
with 19 participants, comparing ensemble-Sankey to traditional Sankey and static 
call graphs. The results show that ensemble-Sankey outperforms the other methods in 
terms of accuracy, efficiency, and user satisfaction, with participants finding it 
more intuitive and easier to navigate.

Pretrained language models achieve impressive results in various NLP tasks,
primarily due to their capacity to learn general representations applicable
across numerous tasks. However, their performance heavily relies on the quality
of the training data, which often contains inherent biases affecting model output.
In this research, we examine the impact of biased training datasets on language
models, specifically highlighting issues that arise when using dynamic datasets,
such as news articles, which continuously evolve with new developments in specific
fields. By utilizing the evolving news corpus, news2tree, which provides in-depth
insights into news articles and serves as a more structured data source,
we investigate the differences between models trained on news2tree and the full
corpus in handling news tasks, and find that models trained on news2tree
outperform their counterparts, and also observe that the news2tree dataset
exhibits significant bias related to the COVID-19 pandemic, which affects
the models' performance, and further investigate the bias through a new metric,
the Token Context Activation Index (TCI), which quantifies the likelihood
of a token being activated by a given context, and demonstrate that
the TCI metric can be used to identify and reduce biases in models, and
the code used in this research is publicly available.

Research on quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in solar and stellar flares has revealed the presence of these phenomena in various solar structures and phenomena, such as sunspots and flares. QPPs have been linked to magnetic reconnection and turbulent magnetic fields, and their occurrence has been observed in various contexts, including the solar corona, sunspots, and even in the magnetosphere of distant planets. The study of QPPs has significant implications for understanding the dynamics of magnetic fields and plasma within these systems. This review provides an overview of the latest findings on QPPs, highlighting recent research in this field.

Anomaly detection in images can be defined as identifying and highlighting the unusual components within a given image category, where normal image samples exhibit consistent characteristics. Various image anomaly detection methods have been developed, yet their performance is often evaluated using standardized datasets that may not accurately reflect the complexities of real-world image anomalies. This paper introduces an open-source platform that enables the assessment of anomaly detection methods in diverse real-world scenarios, utilizing a wide range of publicly accessible image categories. We apply and test several leading anomaly detection methods on this platform, providing an in-depth analysis of their performance across different image categories and comparing their effectiveness in detecting anomalies.

This research investigates the well-posedness of the dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev–Petviashvili I equations in weighted Besov spaces for a specified range of exponents. Our findings demonstrate the preservation of strong stability in this context, which is notable given the known unsolvability of similar equations in unweighted spaces. Additionally, we are able to obtain the solution in the $L^2$ space and establish the equivalence between the $H^s$ and $B^s_{p,1}$ norms of the initial condition, with $s$ constrained by a specified range.

We propose a novel method for designing non-symmetrical energy spectra in systems of fermions that disperse in a three-dimensional space. The proposed approach is grounded in a modified version of Kramers' theorem applicable to non-self-interacting fermion systems with a non-integrable dispersion relation. The method enables the creation of a wide array of energy spectrum configurations, including the introduction of energy level degeneracy, the formation of energy bands, and the existence of energy gaps. Theoretical models of this type hold potential for investigation and might be relevant to the study of systems such as those found in nonlinear wave theories, topological insulators, and the physics of cold atoms.

A novel approach to channel estimation in massive MIMO systems, particularly in scenarios with high mobility, involves a deep learning-based framework. This method incorporates a recurrent neural network and a convolutional neural network to predict channels and a fully connected neural network to predict channel correlation matrices. By leveraging both spatial and temporal channel characteristics, this framework achieves improved performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional methods, particularly in systems with high mobility, and that its performance can be further enhanced through the use of pre-trained networks and feature weighting techniques.

This research paper explores the spatial dimensions of income inequality in Spain, focusing on the 1995 and 2010 periods. By applying both spatial lognormal and spatial generalized beta mixtures, we obtain a more accurate understanding of regional income distributions. The study examines the spatial patterns of income inequality across different regions, investigates the relationship between inequality and the size and economic development of local areas, and analyzes the impact of agglomeration economies on the spatial correlation of income differences.

Given a real-analytic compact manifold M and a point p in M, we define the Grauert tube of p in M as a complex manifold. We then define the operator A on this Grauert tube and show that it satisfies a specific property. Next, we introduce a function of two variables and compute its Bochner mean, providing a partial derivative expression. We also derive an inequality for a specific function value on the Grauert tube, improving an existing result and providing a specific bound with an exact recovery rate. We further establish the upper and lower bounds of a specific operator norm. We also consider the case where M is a compact Einstein manifold and compute the Grauert tube's and Bochner mean's bounds in this scenario, providing a specific inequality. We also establish the lower bound of a specific operator norm in this scenario.

We introduce MARINLINGA, a linear-time algorithm that efficiently computes the reverse line graph of a given graph G, outperforming a previous linear-time algorithm by Wang, Liao, and Poon. The new algorithm is also unique in its simplicity, requiring no pre-processing or advanced data structures, and is easily understood by those familiar with the original line graph algorithm. Additionally, MARINLINGA has been proven to perform optimally in its worst-case scenario with G being a path graph.
This paper validates Lee-Lee's hypothesis, which states that roots related to non-self-intersecting curves in an n-holed sphere equate to real Schur roots in an acyclic quiver with n vertices.

To improve the efficiency of software development, applications are frequently built using pre-existing code libraries. Over time, these dependencies often accumulate changes, ultimately becoming bloated and hindering application maintenance. To address this issue, we propose an approach that employs static code analysis to identify unused dependencies and prioritizes removal based on a dependency's contribution to the application's overall functionality. Our method calculates a dependency's impact by analyzing how much code it influences and the number of times it is accessed. Our experiments on a collection of large Java applications revealed that removing unused dependencies consistently reduces code size. Furthermore, this approach yields a clear understanding of which dependencies are essential to the application, allowing developers to refine their library selection.

The average amount of shared ancestry between a randomly chosen group of chains from a random mixture of several polymer chains, each with a finite number of units, can be calculated using the concept of the average degree of relatedness. This can be achieved by considering the average influence of a specific chain segment. To calculate the average influence of a chain segment, we first derive the average bond between two points within an ABA triad model, followed by the average influence of a chain segment at a specific point on another chain, in cases of both the homopolymer and copolymer mixtures.

We're investigating multistage decision-making problems where uncertainties arise from scenario paths within a probability space. Our goal is to find robust paths that achieve the best average outcome across various scenarios. We've developed a method to solve this type of problem by using empirical scenarios and a variational formulation of distributionally robust multistage optimization. This involves solving a stochastic programming problem in each scenario and then combining the associated sample affine decisions across all scenarios. We've demonstrated that our method converges to the ideal scenario path limit as more scenarios are considered. Furthermore, we've established that our method can be solved using cutting-edge conic solvers and provided computational results to support our findings.

This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal action detection by combining the generation of future video features and action prediction in a single recurrent neural network framework. By utilizing a BiGRU architecture, we efficiently produce future video features, which are then used to propagate decision scores using a novel temporal propagation module. We evaluate our method on the EPIC-KITCHENS dataset and show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

The rapid thermalization of many-body quantum systems is a fundamental phenomenon. A precise definition of thermalization in these systems is formulated using the spectral form factor, which is a measure of how quickly fluctuations diminish in a complex system. A thermalizing system exhibits a phase transition in this measure at late times, during which fluctuations approach those of a thermal ensemble, scaled according to the system's size. Our research demonstrates that this phenomenon occurs in a 2-dimensional lattice of interacting particles connected by random, one-dimensional chains, as the ratio of the chain length to the lattice size becomes extremely large. This is the first example of a 2-dimensional lattice system that exhibits deep thermalization without relying on the properties of higher-dimensional systems. Additionally, we have found a new type of phase transition in a 2-dimensional system, where the fluctuations of eigenbrat states transition from chaotic to ordered behavior, occurring before the thermalization of the system.

We establish the conditions for pseudo-differential operators to be bounded on homogeneous trees and in their $L^p$-weighted counterparts, as well as in their $H^\infty$-weighted counterparts for $p\in[1,\infty]$. Additionally, we explore the conditions for these operators to be compact.

The increasing adoption of 5G technology has led to a significant rise in the number of exposure-strength hotspots, necessitating a shift from exposing users primarily to cell towers to a more widespread distribution. As a result, users are now exposed to a larger number of electromagnetic fields, with research indicating that mobile devices are now the primary point of EMF exposure. To assess the effects of this change, a study was conducted to compare the exposure levels experienced by users in two scenarios: (1) a controlled environment where the exposure to a specific site was maximized, and (2) a more realistic real-world scenario. The study utilized a 5G NR system to measure EMF levels in both scenarios and found that in real-world conditions, users are exposed to a larger number of EMF sources at lower intensity compared to a controlled environment. The study's findings have implications for future research on the effects of EMF exposure.

Deep neural networks often produce inaccurate predictions outside their trained scope. To mitigate this issue, we suggest generating a set of artificial examples, called CODEs, to counter confidently incorrect OOD predictions. We accomplish this by employing a generative adversarial network, trained on the in-distribution data, to produce CODEs. When these CODEs are fed into the DNN, they yield accurate predictions within the CODE set. We then implement a thresholding strategy to differentiate between confident and uncertain predictions. Experimental results indicate that our method successfully decreases the number of overconfident OOD predictions while maintaining a high accuracy rate for in-distribution data, as demonstrated through our experiments on the CIFAR-10/OOD and ImageNet/OOD benchmarks.

Research on azimuthal jet correlations in mid-rapidity proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV has been conducted using the ALICE detector's inner tracking device and CASTOR calorimeter. Data was collected for jets with 15-60 GeV transverse momentum and analyzed for a CASTOR detector forward azimuthal angle. Results reveal a significant reduction in sensitivity due to the internal absorption of energy by the detector. After adjusting for this effect, the data was compared to QCD calculations incorporating non-global QCD predictions and found to be consistent.

Deep learning models can be enhanced using semi-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques that utilize unlabeled data to improve generalizability. However, these methods often come with a significant computational burden and require significant memory. In this study, we introduce a novel memory-efficient approach to implementing semi-supervised learning (SSL) using a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture. By integrating a teacher model and a student model, this framework enables online knowledge transfer and adapts the teacher's predictions to the student's loss, while also allowing the selection of suitable unlabeled examples. To optimize memory usage, we propose two strategies: pruning and quantization. The pruned MoE model can be efficiently integrated into existing deep learning frameworks, as demonstrated by our results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, which show that the pruned model with 16,000 parameters outperforms previous methods with 100,000 parameters.

The goal of anomaly detection is to identify unusual data points in a given dataset based on a reference of normal data, often referred to as the inliers. Current methods for detecting such outliers focus on learning a distance metric from inliers to locate data points that deviate from this metric. However, these approaches may not be effective when dealing with datasets that contain multiple, diverse types of anomalies or high-dimensional data, as these can result in distance metrics that are too restrictive. To address these issues, we propose a new approach called REFAOD, which utilizes reconstruction errors as features to detect anomalies. By incorporating these error features into standard distance metrics, we demonstrate that they can help to relax the assumption of distance metrics being suitable for all types of data. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be applied to both unsupervised and semi-supervised outlier detection settings. Experimental results on real-world benchmark datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in detecting anomalies.

This paper examines a generalized nonlinear complex abstract boundary value problem, exploring its existence, uniqueness, and periodic solutions via a fixed point method. It is established that the problem has a mild solution under certain conditions, and we find that this solution will be classical in certain cases. An example is provided to validate the obtained results.

We examine the possibility of neutrinos being coupled to photons and the constraints from associated processes. This is achieved by considering the presence of light, scalar particles mediating these interactions. The process of neutrino-to-photon conversion occurs via the creation and annihilation of these mediator particles. The current experimental and theoretical limitations on these coupling parameters are determined from constraints on the creation and decay processes of particles like neutrino and photon. The process of neutrino-to-photon conversion within a magnetic field is also studied and the constraints from this effect are derived. Ultimately, the impact of these interactions on the creation of baryon asymmetry is investigated.

The significance of glial cells in the brain has long been debated, with many researchers now accepting that these cells play a key role in neural activity and learning processes.  Although the exact mechanisms by which glial interactions affect neural activity are still not well understood, recent research has shed new light on this mystery.  This review aims to synthesize the current knowledge on how these interactions impact learning, taking into account both the complex dynamics of neural networks and the behavior of single neurons.  By exploring the various theoretical frameworks that have been developed, we can better understand the observed experimental findings, and in turn, these insights can inform the design of future learning algorithms both for neural models and artificial neural networks.

In a study of a magnetic vortex field, we investigated how a neutral particle interacts with its surroundings when passing through a double-slit barrier. Our research revealed that the particle exhibits interference, and the resulting pattern on a screen after the slit barrier includes an additional central bright spot, in addition to the typical interference pattern. Furthermore, we found that the bright spot's intensity depends on the particle's spin and its orientation relative to the vortex field, and that it can potentially dominate the interference pattern for specific parameters.

We explore the probability $F_n(t)$ of a Brownian particle reaching a moving boundary for the $n$th time as time passes. The particle's position is influenced by a moving boundary $x_0(t)$, with the particle's dynamics being governed by the Brownian motion equation within the region $x>x_0(t)$ and absorption at $x_0(t)$ with a reflection coefficient $R$. Our analysis focuses on the scaling of $F_n(t)$ for large $n$ and provides a thorough examination of the impact of the moving boundary and reflection conditions on this scaling behavior.

This research explores the connection between the formal semigroups of L-space knots and their associated Alexander polynomials. The study reveals that for a vast collection of L-space knots, the semigroups are partially separable, with separability tied to the knot's Alexander polynomial's greatest common divisor. Moreover, the research establishes that for a subset of the L-space knots, the semigroups are fully separable, with separability contingent upon the existence of a specific number related to the knot's Alexander polynomial.

This study delves into the long-term behavior of a compressible fluid system's evolution when viscosity effects become negligible. Under these conditions, the system's dynamics are governed by a system of Euler equations with source terms stemming from thermal pressure gradients. We establish the existence of weak solutions for an initial-boundary value problem formulated in a bounded domain with volume-preserving boundary conditions. Notably, the solution sequence exhibits a lack of uniform convergence to a weak solution of the Euler equations as viscosity tends to zero.

Object detection is a crucial component in computer vision, and deep-learning methods have significantly enhanced its capabilities. Nevertheless, the complexity of deep models makes it difficult to obtain reliable results. This paper presents an ensemble deep-learning approach, which integrates multiple state-of-the-art deep models to produce accurate object detection outcomes. The approach, which is adaptable to various model configurations, maximizes the collective strengths of the individual models while mitigating their weaknesses. The proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness in improving the performance of existing object detection methods on VOT2018 and PASCAL VOC 2012 datasets under different configurations.

In recent years, research has shown that code readability is significantly influenced by the quality of its identifiers. To better understand naming conventions in software systems, this study analyzed over 1 million unique identifiers from open-source Java projects hosted on GitHub. Our findings reveal distinct naming patterns for different types of identifiers, such as class and attribute names, which differ in their tendency to use single or multiple words. Additionally, we examined the word usage frequency within these identifier types and found that certain words, like "info" and "util," are commonly reused across different contexts.

A comprehensive study was conducted on the development of grain size and the arrangement of grains in different microstructures during a heat treatment process. The study focused on a specific type of stainless steel alloyed with 18% chromium and 12% tungsten. The research examined the development of grain structures in tripolar, dipolar, and triplex microstructures after being heat-treated at varying temperatures. The study found that the overall growth rate of the grains in these different microstructures followed the same trend, which was influenced by the temperature. The study also found that the shape of the grains in these microstructures remained consistent, regardless of the temperature or configuration of the grains.
